---
title: "Quiz: the snake as a linear system"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. $A$ is the snake matrix (internal force $= -A\mathbf x$), with eigenvalues $\lambda_k = 4\alpha\sin^2(\pi k/n) + 16\beta\sin^4(\pi k/n)$.

---

**Q1.** Why does every row of $A$ sum to zero?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The internal energy depends only on differences between bead positions. Moving the whole snake by the same amount changes nothing, so it creates no force: $A\mathbf 1 = 0$, and the eigenvalue of the constant mode is $\lambda_0 = 0$.
:::

---

**Q2.** What do the corner entries of $A$ (top right, bottom left) represent?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The wrap-around of the closed curve: the last bead is a neighbour of the first. Without them $A$ would be banded and describe an open chain with free ends.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why are the eigenvectors of $A$ sampled cosines and sines?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Every row is the same stencil, shifted by one.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$A\mathbf x$ is a circular convolution of $\mathbf x$ with a fixed stencil. Convolution turns into multiplication in the Fourier basis (*Images in frequency space*): a wave going $k$ times around the curve comes out as the same wave times a number, $\lambda_k$.
:::

---

**Q4.** $\alpha = 0.5$, $\beta = 0.25$. What is the largest step $\tau$ for which the explicit update is stable?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\lambda_\text{max} = 4 \cdot 0.5 + 16 \cdot 0.25 = 6$; stable for $\tau\lambda_\text{max} < 2$, i.e. $\tau < 1/3$.
:::

---

**Q5.** Which pattern of the beads is the first to explode when $\tau$ is too large, and what does it look like?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The mode with the largest eigenvalue, $k = n/2$: alternate beads displaced in opposite directions, a **zig-zag**. Its factor per step $1 - \tau\lambda_\text{max}$ drops below $-1$ first, so it flips sign and grows every step.
:::

---

**Q6.** The semi-implicit step costs a linear solve per step. Why is that cheap?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The matrix $A + \gamma I$ is the same in every step as long as $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\tau$ and $n$ do not change: it can be factored (or inverted) once. It is banded with five diagonals plus corners, so a solve costs a few operations per bead, and $x$ and $y$ use the same factorisation.
:::

---

**Q7.** A balloon snake inflates nicely inside a cell but escapes where the membrane is faint. Name two things you could change.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Lower $\kappa$ (but then it may stop early on the strong side or on texture), raise the edge weight $w$ or lower $\sigma$ where the faint edge needs sharpening, switch to GVF without a balloon, or add shape knowledge (a shape model). No single $\kappa$ fits a strong and a weak edge at once.
:::

---

**Q8.** What does gradient vector flow add that a larger $\sigma$ does not?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
GVF spreads the edge force into flat regions **without** blurring the edges themselves: near edges the field stays equal to the sharp edge force. It also points into concavities, where the plain edge force points sideways. A larger $\sigma$ widens the pull but blurs and shifts the edges and merges nearby ones.
:::

---

**Q9.** Two touching nuclei, one snake around both. Can GVF or a balloon make the snake separate them?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. One snake is one closed curve; no force changes that. It needs two snakes (one started in each nucleus), or an implicit representation that can split (level sets).
:::

---

**Q10.** *(math)* Show that the semi-implicit factor $\gamma/(\gamma + \lambda_k)$ lies in $(0, 1]$ for every $\gamma > 0$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$A$ is positive semidefinite, so $\lambda_k \ge 0$. With $\gamma > 0$: $0 < \gamma \le \gamma + \lambda_k$, hence $0 < \gamma/(\gamma + \lambda_k) \le 1$, with 1 only for $\lambda_k = 0$ (translation).
:::
